title: Stress Recovery during Exposure to Nature Sound and Environmental Noise
research_question: To compare the effects of different sound conditions (nature sound vs. environmental noise) on the rate of physiological recovery after psychological stress, specifically focusing on sympathetic and parasympathetic activation.

participants.description: 40 university students (24 women, 18 men, mean age = 27 years) with hearing thresholds lower than 25 dB in their best ear for all tested frequencies (0.125, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 kHz).
participants.recruitment: Participants received course credit for their participation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Nature sound: A mixture of sounds from a fountain and tweeting birds, with an average sound pressure level of 50 dB (LAeq,4min).
High noise: Road traffic noise recorded close to a densely trafficked road, with an average sound pressure level of 80 dB (LAeq,4min).
Low noise: The same road traffic noise as 'High noise', but set to a lower average sound pressure level of 50 dB (LAeq,4min).
Ambient noise: A recording from a quiet backyard, with a constant low level ambient noise mainly caused by ventilation systems, with an average sound pressure level of 40 dB (LAeq,4min).

measures.instrument: High Frequency Heart Rate Variability (HF HRV)

findings.quote: The perceptual assessment of the sounds showed that the nature sound was perceived as more pleasant than the noises (Figure 2).
the high noise sound was rated as the least pleasant sound.
The perceptual evaluation also showed that the high noise was perceived as more eventful than the other sounds.
The ambient noise was the least eventful and also the least familiar sound, probably because it contained no distinct sound sources
The ambient noise was the least eventful and also the least familiar sound, probably because it contained no distinct sound sources

findings.antecedent: Sound condition (Nature, High noise, Low noise, Ambient noise)
findings.consequent: Mean Skin Conductance Level (SCL) during recovery
findings.quote: The main effect of sound was significant (F3,105 = 2.731, p = 0.048).
effect_size_assumptions: F-test has df1 > 1 (omnibus); d is an approximate directional effect.

findings.consequent: Mean Skin Conductance Level (SCL) during recovery
findings.quote: Pairwise comparisons (t-tests) showed that mean SCL was lower for Nature than High noise (p = 0.045)

findings.antecedent: Sound condition (Nature, High noise, Low noise, Ambient noise) x Time
findings.quote: the interaction between sound and time was significant (F69,2622 = 1.34, p = 0.034). This finding suggests that recovery time for SCL differed among the sound conditions.
effect_size_assumptions: F-test has df1 > 1 (omnibus); d is an approximate directional effect.

findings.mechanism: related to positive emotions (pleasantness) evoked by the nature sound
findings.quote: half-life SCL recovery was 9-37% faster during the nature sound than during the noises.

findings.mechanism: increased arousal due to prolonged exposure to unpleasant noise
findings.quote: The high noise had the longest half life of 159.8 s

findings.mechanism: lack of distinct sound sources causing increased mental activity and SCL

findings.antecedent: Sound condition (Nature, High noise, Low noise, Ambient noise)
findings.consequent: High Frequency Heart Rate Variability (HF HRV) during recovery
findings.quote: We found no consistent effect of type of sound on HF HRV. Average HRV values were not higher for nature sound than for the other sounds, and HF HRV for the high noise was not substantially lower than for the other sounds.

mechanisms: Positive emotions (pleasantness) evoked by nature sound facilitate faster physiological recovery from sympathetic arousal.
Lack of distinct sound sources in ambient noise may cause increased mental activity, leading to increased SCL and slower recovery.
Higher sound pressure levels (e.g., high noise) can increase arousal and slow recovery.
moderators: Presentation order of sounds (examined, showed interaction with sound for SCL, reflecting general SCL increase over experiment)
implementation_implications: Recovery from sympathetic activation in urban outdoor areas with mixed nature and traffic sounds would likely be less effective than in areas undisturbed by noise.
The restorative effects of natural sound environments on stress recovery may be greater with longer exposure times and lower sound pressure levels than those tested in this study.

tables.description: Mean, median, max, min and standard deviation (SD) of SCL and HF HRV for participants (n=40) at baseline and during recovery for each sound condition.

limitations: The study used a small set of environmental sounds of short duration, which limits the generalizability of the results.
The nature sound used in the experiment had a relatively high sound pressure level (50 dBA), which might not reflect typical recreational or rural areas.
The lack of effects on HF HRV suggests that sound exposure during recovery may not strongly influence parasympathetic activity with the specific exposures and physiological indexes used.
Reliable statistical testing of individual half-life SCL values was not possible due to complex numbers generated by estimated constants.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Research suggests that visual impressions of natural compared with urban environments facilitate recovery after psychological stress. To test whether auditory stimulation has similar effects, 40 subjects were exposed to sounds from nature or noisy environments after a stressful mental arithmetic task. Skin conductance level (SCL) was used to index sympathetic activation, and high frequency heart rate variability (HF HRV) was used to index parasympathetic activation. Although HF HRV showed no effects, SCL recovery tended to be faster during natural sound than noisy environments. These results suggest that nature sounds facilitate recovery from sympathetic activation after a psychological stressor.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural environments (including sounds) can restore directed attention capacity after mental fatigue.
Exposure to natural environments (including sounds) can reduce physiological and psychological stress.

mechanism_chain.description: Nature sounds are perceived as pleasant and non-threatening, leading to reduced physiological arousal and improved stress recovery.
